**As the digital realm continues to encompass the corporeal, we’re encountering new problems that no one seems to know the answer to**. Not the overarching brushstrokes of policy and technology, but the nitty-gritty interpersonal issues that it brings us: the dance of flirting on Hinge, keeping tabs on our loved ones via Find My Friends, knowing the right time to Venmo request. Loneliness, love, money, fear, anger, yearning — now through the kaleidoscope of the infinite scroll.

This corner of _it’s steffi_ aims to address life within the social media age, and offer a little advice about how to deal with our most online quandaries. Once a month, I’ll answer a question you have, and perhaps invite some other internet culture friends to share their thoughts, too. If you’d like to submit a question, you can submit through [this form](https://forms.gle/NMvsZhPgHEbva3M68).

Today, our question is answered by [Kelsey Weekman](https://twitter.com/kelsaywhat), senior culture reporter at Yahoo News. Kelsey’s writing has appeared in BuzzFeed News, New York Magazine, Rolling Stone, Billboard, and CBS News. Check out her newsletter, [Okay Zoomer,](https://okayzoomer.substack.com/) which unpacks online youth culture.

* * *

##### _Dear Kelsey,_

#### _**Is there any good way to respond to someone’s Instagram story to start a conversation, or are they all cringe?**_

##### _— Will_

[Leave a comment](https://stefficao.substack.com/p/is-there-a-non-cringe-way-to-swipe/comments)

* * *

Hi sweet one,

Not to immediately get philosophical on you, but existence itself is cringe. Making yourself vulnerable to judgement of any kind can always be misconstrued as posturing or trying too hard, even if you’re not trying to. Set yourself free from the shackles of cringe.

Let’s think about what Instagram is in the first place: a directory of people and places and things where you only see someone’s carefully curated handful of profile posts (and some of the most deranged videos known to man, but we’re not talking about Reels right now). Instagram was once rife with burnt-out filters and song lyric captions paired with whatever in-the-moment image felt memorable, ‘til it morphed into a glorified address book of acquaintances and restaurants. Now its main mode of sharing for most is the story—the fleeting missive about what you’ve seen or experienced or harvested from the timeline lately. What precious digital scrapbook have we lost from the transient nature of Instagram stories? What shared memories have slipped through our fingers because we were afraid to be perceived?

We’re never going to get Old Instagram back, and we might be actively force-fed ads and influencer content and content from our friends posing as influencers because behaving naturally online seems kind of impossible at this point…but come with me now to the realm of earnestness. Imagine we grasped at the interaction available to us online, let things last a little longer, or lingered on the stories it’s so easy to tap through. What if we took posts for what they are—a way of presenting ourselves to the world for interaction, sharing memories and little moments of emotion—and treated them with gentleness instead of judgment? Like precious digital crafts being offered up to us as tiny gifts.

Simply put, if someone has posted something on their Instagram story, they would like people to engage with it. If you’re seeing it, they’ve been vulnerable enough to share something they care about, and they’re inviting the world to interact. Replying to Instagram stories is genuinely one of the great joys of life. It’s fun, largely inconsequential, and even the tiniest bit caring.

Whether you’re thinking about sliding into someone’s DMs in a flirty way or a friendly way, I think one of the most enticing things someone can do is just show that they care. Open yourself up to being what the world might call cringe, but stay steady in your earnestness, and remember that caring is pretty much the most enticing thing a person can do. When replying to an Instagram story, say something that the original poster can respond to, as well. Engage in the conversation that they’ve set up with their post. Having a single glass of wine and swiping up on a bunch of tertiary friends’ Instagram stories is genuinely my ideal night in.

I have amazing news: what other people think about you is literally none of your business. If you’re cringe, who cares? Your fear is probably not of _making_ someone feel uncomfortable, but of feeling uncomfortable yourself. Set that aside. It’s just a feeling, and it’s far less important than a potential connection.

That being said, don’t be weird. Be mindful of why you were invited to the section.

All my love,

Kelsey

# Swipe Up on Instagram: what it is and how to use it in Stories

Written by Growwer · Updated on September 21, 2026

![Swipe Up on Instagram: what it is and how to use it in Stories](/_astro/swipe-up-instagram-en.B0kzyedp.jpg)

Among **the favorites**, Instagram still dominates. In fact, according to statistics for this year, 2022, from the specialized platform Hootsuite, this preference ranking is led by WhatsApp (15.7%), followed by Instagram (14.8%) and Facebook (14.5%). So mastering all its features is crucial to get the most out of it, and one of the most important concepts is Swipe Up on Instagram.

If this concept is new to you, don't worry! You've probably used it hundreds of times without knowing it, and here we'll explain **what Swipe Up on Instagram is and how to use it in your stories** or your brand's.

## What is Swipe Up on Instagram?

The term **Swipe Up on Instagram** and other social networks means exactly what it says, something as simple as **“sliding upward,”** that upward gesture we make with our finger on the screen now that practically all our devices are touchscreens.

Specifically, on Instagram it's used to **access an external link** that has been added in the app by the user's choice. Features like this deliver very good results for marketing strategies or for promoting an account's websites and blogs when they're cleverly integrated with the content.

## 1 Create an Instagram story

To start creating stories, you have two options: either tap your **profile picture** icon or swipe across the screen from left to right. Once there, you'll be able to add a video, a still image, text, hashtags, locations, GIFs… You'll have different options to build a very complete, personalized base for your story.

## 2 Add the link URL

Once you've added this content the way you like it, it's time to **include the link** you want to share. You can do this by tapping the link icon that appears at the top of the screen along with other options, the one shaped like a chain.

Once you've tapped this option, a window **will appear on your screen** that lets you enter the address you want. It must always be complete, with all its parts, to work properly. Then you just tap the confirm button.

## 3 Edit the story

Once this step is done, you can **keep editing** the story as usual before posting it. You'll be able to add a few more things that fit this **Swipe Up** or highlight a prompt asking users to swipe by adding some text.

## 4 Check that it works

You'll know the link was added correctly before you post the story because the chain icon **will be highlighted.** Once it's live, you can open the story from your profile or someone else's to check that it works properly.

Other than that, the social network **doesn't provide information** or statistics on how many users have opened your Swipe Up on Instagram. If you want to do this kind of tracking, you'll have to use an external app designed for social media monitoring and tracking.

## How to use Swipe Up on Instagram in stories

**Swipe Up on Instagram** can only **be used in stories**, since this feature can't be added to the permanent image posts you publish on your feed. Stories are meant for ephemeral content that points to something external. To help you fully understand it, we'll show you step by step how to use it in stories.

Remember that stories are the content that appears at the top of the screen and that they're ephemeral: they **last 24 hours** and then disappear completely from the social network. You can extend their life by adding them to your highlights so they appear on your profile below your bio and above your recent posts.

## What to use Swipe Up on Instagram for

This feature makes sense in certain cases. It's not meant to be overused by posting links constantly for no reason. As with all the options the social network offers, the ideal is to use them as part of a strategy and choose what fits best at each moment.

Here's **what you can use** **Swipe Up on Instagram** for:

*   To expand on the information in a story.
*   To direct users to an offer you're promoting.
*   To introduce them to a new website or blog from your brand.
*   To give them access to external forms.
*   To showcase other brands you collaborate with.

Ideally, if it doesn't fit any of these situations, skip using Swipe Up on Instagram. Otherwise it will come across as **too gratuitous** or overly promotional, and it won't interest your followers.

It's also a good idea to create some sort **of anticipation** so swiping feels appealing. For example, by sharing a bit of information and adding a line like “discover more” or “swipe up for all the details” to spark interest in reading or watching the rest of the content.

## New Instagram feature for adding links to stories

**Instagram is constantly updating** and changes some of its options to improve the user experience or simply as an experiment. One of the **latest changes** has been precisely the replacement of this Swipe Up with the link sticker.

If you open Instagram now and go to the story creation screen, you'll find something new. When you tap the icon at the top right, a drop-down menu will appear with the **different options such as GIFs, music and locations.**  
In that same drop-down you'll see a **sticker that says “link”**. If you select it, you just have to enter the link and it will appear in the new format integrated into your story.
